11. Reusable studies and standalone verbs

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-11-parameters.Rmd
book-11-parameters.Rmd

What you will learn

Bind typed parameters, use omop_study and shortcuts, then derive and filter columns without bringing rows to your computer.

This chapter uses the public synthetic Synthea27Nj numeric connection from Getting started.

You need: the packages and the matching practice connection described in Before you start. Run its sections in order. Each chapter starts from a fresh practice connection; all the outputs below come from real dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.5 calls. The numbers describe teaching data, not clinical findings.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the book-work directory created in Getting started. Run this setup first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/connection.R")
source("tools/book/practice.R")
practice <- if (book_driver == "DSLite") book_practice("numeric") else book_connect("numeric")
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

The site connection is ready. The shared connection.R selects DSLite or Opal and resolves the resource names.

Describe the setting as a parameter

A parameter is a named, typed placeholder in a study definition. It lets you reuse a recipe without editing its logic. It is not R code or SQL text.

setting <- omop_param("setting", type = "concept_set")
class(setting)
#> [1] "omop_param" "list"

This parameter accepts concept sets. A separate date parameter would declare a date type; give each changing input its own appropriate type.

Build a template 

template <- omop_study(omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = setting),
  outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
    prior_visits = omop_count("visit_occurrence", window = omop_window(-365, -1)),
    age = omop_age()))
class(template)
#> [1] "omop_recipe" "list"

omop_study() returns an ordinary recipe. It creates an indexed population and baseline output. We explicitly exclude day zero from the prior-visit count. The unbound template cannot execute until its required setting is supplied.

Bind and inspect 

outpatient <- recipe_bind(template, setting = 9202L)
class(outpatient)
#> [1] "omop_recipe" "list"

Binding fills the placeholder while preserving the template. Concept 9202 is the outpatient visit setting, not the record’s provenance type.

book_symbols(recipe_execute(outpatient, out = c(baseline = "D_param_outpatient"), conns = conns))
#>             baseline 
#> "D_param_outpatient"
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_param_outpatient$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 28
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#>  0.000000  0.000000  0.750000  3.500000 17.000000 18.000000 18.000000  8.071429

The server computes annual age (index year minus birth year) at the first outpatient visit. The analyst receives only the approved summary.

Read the simple-layer defaults 

print(outpatient)
#> Concept presentation: factors; identity is the declared concept class, preserved through aliases and value-preserving reducers.
#> Label precedence: variable recode, recipe recode, vocabulary name, decimal ID fallback. Explicit equal recodes merge categories.
#> Federation: permitted ID union, including declared unused levels; newest comparable vocabulary version, then bytewise name tie. Unresolved versions never establish recency.
#> Generated names: ASCII snake_case vocabulary tokens; colliding automatic names gain concept-ID suffixes. Vocabulary-dependent names are unresolved until permitted federation reconciliation.
#> variables.prior_visits: concept origin follows reducer count over the declared source value; explicit variable name is retained. 
#> === omop_recipe ===
#> Populations ( 2 ):
#>    base  :  All Persons 
#>    study  :  Base Population 
#> Variables ( 2 ):
#>    prior_visits :  count of visit_occurrence 
#>    age :  derived age (exact annual age) 
#> Filters ( 0 ):
#> Outputs ( 1 ):
#>    baseline  [ wide ] pop: study 
#> Study 'study' (omop_study()) defaults chosen:
#>   - index selection "first" (default): the first candidate per person, selected before the requirements
#>   - observation coverage unique/drop/drop (default)
#>   - every output has episode grain; survival ties follow the priority rule; dates are relative to the index date (simple-layer choices)

The study’s default index selection is first. The population uses the default coverage policy; all requirements are combined with AND. Baseline has episode rows. For survival, supply outcomes and an explicit follow-up definition. For example, follow_up = list(start = 1, end = 365, censor = c("observation_end", "death")) describes a year after entry, ending sooner at a listed censor. The output chapter executes the corresponding native survival format.

Shortcuts expand into ordinary variables

Use a shortcut when its defaults match your question; use an explicit reducer when you need more control. before = 365 includes day zero, while after = 365 starts at day one. Without either, most shortcuts use all history through entry.

shortcuts <- omop_study(omop_event("measurement", 3000963L), outputs = "baseline",
  baseline = list(ever = omop_ever("measurement", 3000963L, before = 365),
    count = omop_count("measurement", 3000963L, before = 365),
    value = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3000963L,
      tolerance = c(-30, 0), unit = 8713L)))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(shortcuts, out = c(baseline = "D_shortcuts"), conns = conns))
#>      baseline 
#> "D_shortcuts"
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_shortcuts$ever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
#> $output.list
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props
#>                 study
#> D_shortcuts$ever site
#>                1    1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props
#>                 study
#> D_shortcuts$ever site
#>                1    1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
#>                 study
#> D_shortcuts$ever site
#>                1   28
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_proportions
#> D_shortcuts$ever
#> 1 
#> 1 
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_shortcuts$ever
#>  1 
#> 28 
#> 
#> 
#> $validity.message
#> [1] "Data in all studies were valid"

Everyone has ever = 1 because the index hemoglobin measurement itself is included. To ask about measurements strictly before entry use window = omop_window(-365, -1) instead. First/last/mean/min/max-value shortcuts use the same event and window model. omop_history() bundles named ever variables; it does not define a new language.

What the mutate contract means

ds.omop.mutate() creates or replaces columns on a private omop.table. Although its notation looks like R, the client sends a mutate data request: the server validates a closed grammar and column types. It never runs arbitrary R code. Bare names refer to columns, including earlier assignments in the same call; literal numbers, strings, booleans and missing values are allowed.

The grammar supports +, -, *, /, comparisons of a column with a literal, ifelse, case_when, coalesce, and cut with public breaks. Date subtraction returns days; adding an integer to a date returns a date. Division by zero or nonfinite arithmetic gives missing values. Person, episode and set keys and other protected columns cannot be read or written; class-1 source names are also refused. Privacy explains those protections.

For derivation inside a new recipe, prefer the native expressions taught in Derived numeric formulas. This chapter deliberately teaches standalone mutation of an already assigned table, including sequential assignments, new objects and rollback. Those remain useful operations.

Prepare weight and height at the same date

BMI is weight in kilograms divided by squared height in metres. Index each person at their first weight measurement, then select weight and height on that date. We require the recorded kg and cm units; we do not combine unrelated latest readings or silently substitute a height from another day.

weight_event <- omop_event("measurement", 3025315L)
body <- omop_study(weight_event, outputs = "baseline", baseline = list(
  weight_kg = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3025315L,
    tolerance = c(0, 0), unit = 9529L),
  height_cm = omop_value_at_index("measurement", 3036277L,
    tolerance = c(0, 0), unit = 8582L),
  age = omop_age_at(omop_anchor(weight_event)),
  first_date = omop_date(omop_anchor(weight_event, which = "first")),
  last_date = omop_date(omop_anchor(weight_event, which = "last"))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(body, out = c(baseline = "D_body"), conns = conns))
#> baseline 
#> "D_body"

These are synthetic Synthea measurements, including children. Calculated BMI is a numeric teaching example, not an adult clinical classification.

Create a new object 

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_body", height_m = height_cm / 100,
  bmi = weight_kg / (height_m * height_m), newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_bmi"
bmi_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(bmi_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 11.53374
site 10% 13.62216
site 25% 15.88957
site 50% 23.86380
site 75% 27.93787
site 90% 30.20849
site 95% 30.36386
site Mean 22.11315

The second assignment uses the newly created height_m. A missing input gives a missing BMI. newobj = "D_bmi" preserves D_body; neither table is downloaded.

body_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_body", datasources = conns)
bmi_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_bmi", datasources = conns)
c(original_has_bmi = "bmi" %in% body_columns$site,
  new_has_bmi = "bmi" %in% bmi_columns$site)
#> original_has_bmi      new_has_bmi 
#>            FALSE             TRUE

The original has no BMI column, and the new object does.

Group ages with public breaks

Choose boundaries from the study design, not from private minimum/maximum ages. These broad age bands are for teaching. right = FALSE includes the lower bound and excludes the upper bound; ages outside the range remain missing.

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", age_group = cut(age, c(0, 18, 121),
  labels = c("under 18", "18 to 120"), right = FALSE),
  newobj = "D_grouped", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_grouped"
age_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_grouped$age_group",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(age_counts))
Category Count
18 to 120 14
under 18 14
NA 0

cut produces text labels in this grammar, not an ordered R factor. The table may display them alphabetically. Chapter 14 shows how to assign an explicit factor level sequence for modelling and display.

Exercise: create an adult flag using the same lower boundary of 18.

Solution — an age recode

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_grouped", adult = ifelse(age >= 18, "yes", "no"),
  newobj = "D_adults", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_adults"
adult_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_adults$adult", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(adult_counts))
Category Count
no 14
yes 14
NA 0

A missing age stays missing rather than becoming “no”. The adult count equals the 18-to-120 band; the under-18 band becomes “no”.

Subtract dates on the server 

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", span_days = last_date - first_date,
  newobj = "D_span", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_span"
span_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_span$span_days", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(span_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 952.700
site 10% 1845.200
site 25% 6142.500
site 50% 6678.000
site 75% 6996.500
site 90% 7049.000
site 95% 7053.550
site Mean 5679.607

This is elapsed time between first and last recorded weights, in days. It is not age or duration under continuous observation. Exact dates stay private.

Exercise: express that duration in 365-day years, retaining the days column.

Solution — convert a duration

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_span", span_years = span_days / 365,
  newobj = "D_years", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_years"
years_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_years$span_years", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(years_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 2.610137
site 10% 5.055343
site 25% 16.828767
site 50% 18.295890
site 75% 19.168493
site 90% 19.312329
site 95% 19.324794
site Mean 15.560567

Each summary is the day summary divided by 365. These are fixed-length units, not completed birthdays; use omop_age_at for completed age.

Recode with case_when

Cases are checked in order. The first true condition wins. In mutate, an unknown condition gives a missing result immediately, rather than falling through to the default. Handle missingness explicitly when your study needs it.

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", life_stage = case_when(
  is.na(age) ~ "unknown", age < 5 ~ "young child",
  age < 18 ~ "older child", .default = "adult"),
  newobj = "D_stage", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_stage"
stage_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_stage$life_stage",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(stage_counts))
Category Count
adult 14
older child 5
young child 9
NA 0

The declared default applies only after the preceding conditions are false. This recode distinguishes unknown age from a known age; it does not impute age.

Exercise: recode both child labels to “no”, and the adult label to “yes”.

Solution — recode a derived category

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_stage", adult = case_when(
  life_stage %in% c("young child", "older child") ~ "no",
  life_stage == "unknown" ~ NA,
  .default = "yes"), newobj = "D_recoded", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_recoded"
recode_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_recoded$adult", useNA = "always",
  datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(recode_counts))
Category Count
no 14
yes 14
NA 0

These counts agree with the earlier adult flag. Here the synthetic source has complete ages, so the missingness branch introduces no extra category count.

Replace an object in place

Use the same name for x and newobj to replace that server object. Omitting newobj instead generates a fresh name; it does not mean “in place”.

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", height_m = height_cm / 100,
  bmi = weight_kg / (height_m * height_m), bmi_copy = bmi,
  newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_bmi"
before_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_bmi", datasources = conns)
before_bmi <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
c(copy_added = "bmi_copy" %in% before_columns$site,
  bmi_unchanged = identical(bmi_result, before_bmi))
#>    copy_added bmi_unchanged 
#>          TRUE          TRUE

The replacement adds bmi_copy while preserving BMI. The client keeps a rollback copy until all participating sites succeed, restoring originals if assignment fails. This single-site practice example verifies that failure leaves the table usable; it does not simulate a network outage.

Read the refusal messages

The following failures are intentional. First try an unknown function:

unknown_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", bmi = sqrt(bmi), newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(unknown_message, "\n")
#> ds.omop.mutate(): 'sqrt' is not part of the mutation grammar (+ - * /, conditions, ifelse, case_when, coalesce, cut, as.Date).

sqrt is outside the closed grammar and is refused by the client before a request can alter the table. Use supported arithmetic or a documented analysis function; arbitrary R functions cannot be sent through mutate.

Next try to copy a protected key. The server refuses this column reference:

key_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", copied = person_id,
    newobj = "D_key_copy", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(key_message, "\n")
#> OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: column 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be used in an expression; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

A class-1 source name is refused even when used as the name of a new column:

blocked_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", person_source_value = "label",
    newobj = "D_blocked_copy", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(blocked_message, "\n")
#> OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: 'person_source_value' is a blocked (class-1) column name; choose another name; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

This is a blocked source/assignment name, not a request to alter its protection. Use descriptive study-variable names for allowed derived values.

Finally request an ordinary BMI change followed by a protected-key overwrite in the same in-place call. The whole request must fail:

rollback_message <- tryCatch({
  ds.omop.mutate("D_bmi", bmi = bmi + 1, person_id = "replacement",
    newobj = "D_bmi", conns = conns)
  "Unexpected success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(rollback_message, "\n")
#> OMOP mutate failed and 'D_bmi' was left unchanged: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be written; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors()

The protected-identifier message applies to person, episode and set keys and any columns marked protected by the server. It prohibits both reads and writes. Renaming a key is not an allowed transformation.

after_columns <- dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_bmi", datasources = conns)
after_bmi <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
c(columns_preserved = identical(before_columns, after_columns),
  bmi_preserved = identical(before_bmi, after_bmi),
  refused_copies_absent = !any(c("D_key_copy", "D_blocked_copy") %in%
    DSI::datashield.symbols(conns)$site))
#>     columns_preserved         bmi_preserved refused_copies_absent 
#>                  TRUE                  TRUE                  TRUE

All checks are true. Even the earlier bmi + 1 assignment was not committed. These released checks establish schema and summary stability; the book’s synthetic-source verification additionally checks equality of the entire table.

Filter using a predicate

A predicate is a condition. Only TRUE rows survive; missing conditions are dropped. This retains adults without using a key to target a known person.

print(ds.omop.filter("D_bmi", expr = omop_where(age >= 18),
  newobj = "D_adult_bmi", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_adult_bmi"
filtered_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_adult_bmi$bmi", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(filtered_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 22.75976
site 10% 23.69819
site 25% 25.78897
site 50% 28.03959
site 75% 29.79277
site 90% 30.36457
site 95% 30.45801
site Mean 27.34679

The subset meets the distinct-person release threshold in this practice data. It remains a private table. A small or empty final subset can be refused, as chapter 12 demonstrates.

Exercise: keep the adult category from D_stage with the same filter grammar.

Solution — filter a text category

print(ds.omop.filter("D_stage", expr = omop_where(life_stage == "adult"),
  newobj = "D_working_age", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_working_age"
working_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_working_age$bmi", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_summary(working_result))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 22.75976
site 10% 23.69819
site 25% 25.78897
site 50% 28.03959
site 75% 29.79277
site 90% 30.36457
site 95% 30.45801
site Mean 27.34679

This category means ages 18 and over, so its summary agrees with the preceding filter. The earlier missingness case ensures an unknown age is not called adult.

Try it

Bind the same template to inpatient visits and summarise the prior-visit count. Do not alter the outpatient template in place.

Solution

inpatient <- recipe_bind(template, setting = 9201L)
book_symbols(recipe_execute(inpatient, out = c(baseline = "D_param_inpatient"), conns = conns))
#>            baseline 
#> "D_param_inpatient"
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_param_inpatient$prior_visits", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 7
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>        5%       10%       25%       50%       75%       90%       95%      Mean 
#>  2.000000  2.000000  2.500000  6.000000  8.500000 11.000000 12.500000  6.285714

Each binding is a separate recipe. Its own index changes which earlier records fall into the lookback window. A numeric summary suits these varied counts; a categorical table can be refused when it creates too many distinct levels in a small population.

Recap

Parameters change declared inputs, shortcuts express common native recipes, and mutate/filter operate privately on assigned tables. Each final object still passes publication checks.
